strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in RAFT-style optical flow: all-pairs correlation sampling at ultra-high resolution. The proposed block-sparse, patch-major, cached sampling algorithm is well motivated by an empirical analysis of actual correlation access patterns and preserves the same mathematical operator rather than changing the model objective.

The systems contribution is practically meaningful. Isolated benchmarks show large runtime gains over on-demand sampling at high resolutions while avoiding the quadratic memory blow-up of the dense implementation. End-to-end experiments on RAFT, CCMR, MS-RAFT+, and SEA-RAFT demonstrate that the operator can improve feasible high-resolution inference, especially when dense correlation is out of memory.

The manuscript includes useful component analysis, ablations on caching, and additional measurements across image size, feature dimension, iteration count, and several GPU types. This supports the central efficiency claims better than a single benchmark would.

The 8K optical-flow evaluation is a valuable addition. The paper studies how resolution affects accuracy and large-motion behavior across many existing methods, and the cascaded SEA-RAFT inference modification gives a simple, training-free way to reduce large-motion errors at high resolution.
The writing is generally clear, with good diagrams and tables explaining the algorithmic structure, access-pattern motivation, and empirical trade-offs.
weaknesses: The reproducibility of the core contribution is not fully established from the manuscript. The method relies on custom CUDA kernels, block cache management, modified sampled matrix multiplication, and implementation-specific memory behavior, but the paper does not clearly state whether code and the generated 8K dataset will be released. Without these artifacts, reproducing the speed and memory claims would be difficult.

The exact-equivalence claim is only lightly validated. The paper reports unit tests and a near-zero 0.03% EPE difference, but it does not give detailed numerical error bounds for the sampled correlations themselves, effects of padding/block boundaries, bilinear sampling across sparse blocks, or precision differences relative to the official implementation.

The proposed method is not uniformly better: it uses substantially more memory than on-demand sampling at the largest scales and can be slower or neutral on lower-resolution datasets such as Spring, Sintel, and KITTI. The main benefit is therefore concentrated in a specific high-resolution regime, which should be framed more carefully.

The 8K dataset evaluation is useful but narrow: it contains 332 pairs from three rendered CHARGE sequences, uses synthetic forward flow only, and may not represent the diversity of real UHR video, camera motion, or non-rendered artifacts. This limits how strongly the paper can claim state-of-the-art high-resolution optical flow performance in general.

The cascaded SEA-RAFT result is compelling but somewhat entangled with the operator contribution. The accuracy gains primarily come from a test-time inference schedule, while the sampling algorithm mainly affects feasibility and speed. The paper could more cleanly separate these two contributions and clarify which claims depend on each.

Some experimental comparisons are hard to interpret because methods differ in training data, native design assumptions, tiling strategies, feasible resolution, and whether the proposed operator applies. This is partly unavoidable, but it weakens direct ranking claims across all methods.

The complexity analysis is somewhat idealized. It assumes a particular scaling of block size with pixel count and bounded lookup radius, while practical performance depends heavily on flow smoothness, cache growth, sparsity, GPU memory hierarchy, and implementation overheads. The empirical results are more convincing than the asymptotic argument.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in RAFT-style optical flow: dense all-pairs correlation is fast but memory-prohibitive at high resolution, while on-demand correlation saves memory but is slow. The proposed block-sparse, cached sampling implementation is a practically meaningful engineering contribution for ultra-high-resolution inference.

The method is designed to preserve the same mathematical operator as RAFT-style correlation sampling, making it potentially useful as a drop-in replacement for several existing models. The paper reports near-zero endpoint-error difference relative to the official implementation and provides end-to-end measurements on RAFT, CCMR, MS-RAFT+, and SEA-RAFT.

The runtime/memory evidence is fairly extensive for the isolated operator: the paper varies resolution, number of recurrent iterations, feature dimensionality, and GPU model. The reported gains over on-demand sampling are substantial, especially at high resolutions where dense correlation is infeasible.

The 8K optical-flow evaluation is valuable as a stress test. The paper compares a broad set of methods and shows that native-resolution inference can recover fine detail but often harms large-motion estimation, which is a useful empirical observation.

The cascaded SEA-RAFT inference variant is simple but effective in the presented setting, improving large-motion errors without retraining and producing the best reported results on the proposed 8K dataset.
weaknesses: The main algorithmic novelty is limited. The core contribution is largely an implementation strategy combining block-sparse correlation computation, layout changes, and caching. This is useful, but the paper sometimes frames it as a broader algorithmic advance without fully separating conceptual novelty from CUDA/kernel engineering.

The claimed sub-quadratic O(P^1.5) memory complexity is not fully convincing as presented. The derivation depends on choosing block size B = P^(1/8), while the actual experiments use fixed B = 8 or B = 16. With fixed block size, the block mask term still scales quadratically in P up to a constant factor. This makes the asymptotic claim potentially misleading relative to the implemented method.

The reproducibility story is incomplete for a systems contribution. The method depends on custom CUDA kernels and modified sampled block-sparse matrix multiplication, but the manuscript does not clearly state code availability, provide enough low-level implementation details to reimplement performance-critical pieces, or discuss numerical tolerances beyond a brief unit-test/EPE statement.

The 8K benchmark is narrow: it uses 332 forward-flow pairs from three sequences of a single Blender movie. This is useful but not enough to strongly support broad claims about ultra-high-resolution optical flow. The dataset generation modifies scene properties, and the impact of these choices on realism or ground-truth quality is not analyzed in depth.

The “state-of-the-art” claim is mostly on a newly generated synthetic dataset proposed by the authors, not on an established public high-resolution benchmark. This weakens the evidential force of the accuracy claims, especially because the cascaded SEA-RAFT modification is evaluated mainly in this one setting.

The end-to-end speedups are mixed. On low-resolution Sintel/KITTI/Spring, the proposed sampler is often neutral or slower for several RAFT-style methods. Even on the 8K setting, some models see modest or negative improvements, and the method uses substantially more memory than on-demand sampling.

The cascaded inference extension is quite simple and resembles standard coarse-to-fine/warm-start inference. Its effectiveness is worthwhile, but its originality is modest and the paper does not deeply analyze failure cases, sensitivity to the 800px threshold, scale schedule, or why SEA-RAFT benefits more than alternatives.

Some experimental comparisons conflate multiple axes: model architecture, input scale, tiling, correlation backend, and feasibility under an 80GB memory limit. The paper reports many numbers, but the fairness of comparing “highest feasible scale” across methods is debatable because some methods are designed with different memory/speed tradeoffs.

Presentation is generally understandable, but important details are deferred or underspecified: exact cache behavior, proxy-volume construction for bilinear sampling across block boundaries, numerical equivalence tests, and memory accounting would need more precision for a CVPR-level systems/operator paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in RAFT-style optical-flow methods: dense all-pairs correlation is fast but quadratic in memory, while on-demand sampling is memory-efficient but slow. The proposed block-sparse, patch-major, cached sampler is well motivated by an empirical access-pattern analysis showing that only a small fraction of correlation cells are sampled.

The contribution is practically useful because it preserves the exact mathematical correlation-sampling operator used by RAFT-style methods, making it a drop-in implementation improvement rather than an architecture change that trades accuracy for efficiency.

The experimental evidence is substantial for the target setting. Isolated operator benchmarks cover resolution, iteration count, feature dimension, and multiple GPUs; end-to-end experiments show meaningful speedups over on-demand sampling at high resolution and much lower memory than dense correlation.

The 8K optical-flow evaluation is valuable. The dataset has rendered ground truth at ultra-high resolution, includes 332 frame pairs and 9.3B evaluated pixels, and the paper compares a broad set of optical-flow methods across multiple input scales.

The cascaded SEA-RAFT inference extension is simple but effective: it improves large-motion performance at high resolution without retraining and achieves the best reported 1px and large-motion scores in the paper’s 8K evaluation.

The manuscript is generally clear. The algorithmic pipeline, complexity argument, runtime breakdown, and supplementary implementation details make the main idea understandable and reasonably reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: The novelty is more systems/implementation-oriented than conceptual. The main insight is exploiting sparse, regular access to a known correlation operator with block-sparse computation and caching. This is useful, but the algorithmic ingredients are relatively natural once the sampling pattern is observed.

Reproducibility is not fully demonstrated. The method depends on custom CUDA kernels and modified sampled block-sparse matrix multiplication, but the paper only provides pseudocode and high-level implementation details. There is no clear code-release or artifact statement in the manuscript.

The correctness validation is somewhat thin. The paper states that unit tests and endpoint-error comparison show a near-zero 0.03% difference from the official implementation, but it does not report detailed numerical tolerances, exact equivalence tests across boundary cases, or failure cases involving padding, block boundaries, bilinear interpolation, and multi-level pyramids.

The memory/runtime claims need careful interpretation. The proposed method often uses substantially more memory than on-demand sampling, especially at the highest isolated resolutions, while still being far below dense correlation. This is a good trade-off for the target setting, but the abstract-level phrasing may overstate similarity in memory usage to on-demand sampling.

The 8K benchmark is useful but limited in diversity: it is generated from one Blender movie, uses 335 frames/332 pairs, and evaluates only forward flow. This constrains conclusions about general UHR optical-flow performance across domains, camera motions, weather/lighting, and real captured content.

The cascaded inference comparison is not entirely isolated from the operator contribution. Cascaded SEA-RAFT is an additional test-time algorithmic change applied to one baseline, and other methods are not given analogous multi-scale initialization or tuning. This is acceptable as an extra contribution, but it complicates claims of state-of-the-art method-level accuracy.

Low- and standard-resolution results show limited or negative speed impact for several methods on Spring, Sintel, and KITTI. The method is clearly targeted to high resolution, but the paper should more explicitly delimit where the overheads outweigh the benefits.

Some experimental choices could affect fairness or interpretation, including different block sizes for some methods, reliance on PTLFlow checkpoints mostly fine-tuned on Sintel, FlowFormer using its default tiling, and benchmarking on high-memory GPUs that are not typical deployment hardware. These choices are mostly documented, but their impact is not deeply analyzed.
